{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "A has more payer signal than B, though still weak. Funding of $930k flowed into BikeMaps.org from a public health agency, and Pointz runs a premium subscription tier. Money has moved through the category. B shows no one ever paying for Pascal docs, and the Foundation that might pay says it funds development, not docs.",
    "A's acquisition channel is more concrete. Advocacy nonprofits already run hazard-report tools and have dues-paying members, such as the League of American Bicyclists at $50/yr, which points to a partner path to an institutional buyer. B relies on organic forum posting, plus paid search at a generic $2.69 CPC that the brief admits is likely not Pascal-specific.",
    "A's category is larger, and the function has been repeatedly validated: BikeMaps.org, LaneSpotter in 11 cities, Pointz, WABA and the Davis project. B's own case against says the developer population looks too small to sustain revenue for a one-person company.",
    "B's case against undercuts its core premise. A cited thread suggests the bottleneck is maintainer unwillingness to engage with doc fixes, not tooling. An outside site cannot fix that.",
    "Both briefs face entrenched free incumbents. A at least names a testable non-consumer wedge (selling aggregated hazard data to cities or insurers, or a Vision Zero program buyer) for a 90-day sales attempt. B's only wedge is an untested business tier."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's price hypothesis of a ~$50/month business tier is anchored only to Read the Docs' published pricing. That is a competitor's list price, not evidence that any company shipping Lazarus-based products would pay. No such company is named, and no buyer is shown expressing willingness to pay.",
  "confidence_note": "Low-to-moderate confidence. Neither brief shows a paying customer for a product like the proposed one, and both are dominated by free incumbents. A's strongest payer path, municipal Vision Zero programs or research grants, appears only in its 'Case For' with no source, so it counts as missing evidence. Grant cycles and municipal procurement may also be hard to close within 90 days. A wins mainly because B's payer evidence is essentially absent and B's own brief questions whether the problem is solvable with tooling. B's open questions section points to 'the list above', but no list is provided, which makes it thinner still."
}
